content: Women who are older and those attended by doctors tend to have longer hospital stays following uncomplicated, term vaginal births, according to an analysis of data from Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS) across 30 countries. Conversely, women attended by non-skilled staff consistently have shorter stays compared to those attended by nurse-midwives. Wealthier women and those who deliver via cesarean section in private facilities also experience longer stays. Factors such as transportation to outpatient care, childcare for siblings, and income loss due to a partner or family member taking time off work can influence the length of stay and follow-up care. Home visits are recommended to ensure proper follow-up for all mother-infant pairs after discharge. Another study using DHS data from 33 sub-Saharan African countries highlights significant variability in the percentage of women receiving postnatal checks before discharge. Women who are more educated, wealthier, received more antenatal care visits, or had cesarean births are more likely to receive pre-discharge checks. In contrast, women who gave birth in lower-level public facilities or were attended by nurses/midwives rather than doctors are less likely to receive postnatal checks. A study analyzing data from 25 sub-Saharan African countries between 2000 and 2016 found that facility-based births were significantly lower among the poorest women compared to the wealthiest, although wealth-based disparities have decreased over time. Another study using data from 43 DHS surveys (2003–2013) observed increases in facility-based births across Africa and Asia in nearly all wealth groups, urban and rural areas, and public and private facilities. However, socioeconomic differences persist, with wealthier women and those in urban areas more likely to access facility-based care for childbirth. Qualitative evidence synthesis exploring perspectives on discharge indicates that postnatal care for women is often overlooked, with greater emphasis placed on newborn care. There is a common assumption that women receive adequate information during antenatal care, though evidence supporting this is limited. Both women and health workers perceive the discharge process as rushed, with excessive information provided in a short time, compounded by time constraints and workforce shortages. Women and parents express a desire for more knowledge and practical skills related to self-care, newborn care, and managing postpartum depression. They also value engagement and preparation for postnatal care, including tailored education and support. Health workers report a need for more specific guidelines and training to provide effective postnatal education. Women, particularly first-time mothers, may require additional time to process pre-discharge information to feel confident in managing at home. This includes understanding infant behaviors (feeding, sleeping, crying cues) and safety, as well as addressing personal needs such as perineal trauma, pain, wound care, and emotional well-being. The postnatal environment, particularly noisy and disruptive ward conditions, can lead to frustration and early discharge for some women. Feasibility challenges include staff shortages, lack of training, language barriers, financial constraints, and societal norms affecting postnatal education. Administrative duties related to discharge add to health workers' workload, limiting their ability to provide quality, woman-centered care. Building trustful relationships and providing timely, sufficient information are seen as critical by providers. WHO recommendations emphasize assessing maternal and newborn physical and emotional well-being, caregiver skills and confidence, and home environment factors before discharge. Effective counseling and culturally appropriate communication strategies are integral to this process. Evidence from a scoping review on discharge preparation highlights the importance of addressing individual needs and linking families to follow-up care and support. Studies on early discharge following cesarean birth show varied policies, ranging from discharge on the first to third day post-surgery, compared to standard practices of 48 hours to seven days. Maternal mortality within one year post-cesarean was not reported in trials comparing early and usual discharge. Evidence on neonatal mortality and infant readmission for morbidity within seven days is uncertain. Cost outcomes and resource requirements for early discharge policies vary, with no direct evidence on health equity impacts. Additional analyses are needed to assess the effects of early discharge by mode of birth.
